claims.source_text: Almost half (46.8%, n = 487) are Data Deficient (DD) meaning that information is insufficient to assess their status
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct count from IUCN Red List assessments where insufficient data prevented threat categorization.

claims.claim: At least 68 additional Data Deficient species are likely to be threatened based on predictive modeling.
claims.source_text: Of the 487 DD species for which we had sufficient maximum body size (n = 396) and geographic distribution data (n = 378), we were able to predict that at least a further 68 DD species are likely to be threatened
claims.evidence_reasoning: Predictive modeling using maximum body size and geographic distribution to estimate threat status of DD species.

claims.claim: Accounting for Data Deficient species, at least one-quarter (24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened.
claims.source_text: Accounting for the uncertainty in threat levels due to the number of DD species, we estimate that more than half face some elevated risk: at least one-quarter (n = 249; 24%) of chondrichthyans are threatened
claims.evidence_reasoning: Combines observed threatened species (181) with predicted threatened DD species (68) for total estimate.

claims.claim: Only 37% of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be Least Concern.
claims.source_text: Only 37% are predicted to be Least Concern
claims.evidence_reasoning: Prediction based on apportioning Data Deficient species using predictive models.

claims.claim: One-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) are threatened.
claims.source_text: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct count from habitat-specific threat analysis in Table 2.

claims.claim: Almost half of neritic and epipelagic chondrichthyan species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
claims.source_text: By habitat, one-quarter of coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans (26.3%, n = 127 of 482) and almost half of neritic and epipelagic species (43.6%, n = 17 of 39) are threatened.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct count from habitat-specific threat analysis in Table 2.

claims.claim: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family.
claims.source_text: As a result of their high exposure to coastal shallow-water fisheries and their large body size, sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on family-level threat analysis showing highest proportion of threatened species in Pristidae.

claims.claim: Sawfishes are arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes.
claims.source_text: sawfishes (Pristidae) are the most threatened chondrichthyan family and arguably the most threatened family of marine fishes
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison of Pristidae threat levels with other marine fish families, though 'arguably' indicates some uncertainty.

claims.claim: One-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing.
claims.source_text: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting whether species are targeted or bycatch.

claims.claim: Some of the most threatened chondrichthyan species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture (bycatch).
claims.source_text: While one-third of threatened sharks and rays are subject to targeted fishing, some of the most threatened species (including sawfishes and large-bodied skates) have declined due to incidental capture in fisheries targeting other species.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on threat assessments and supported by literature on bycatch impacts.

claims.claim: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37).
claims.source_text: Half of the 69 high-volume or high-value sharks and rays in the global fin trade are threatened (53.6%, n = 37)
claims.evidence_reasoning: Cross-reference of species in fin trade (from Clarke et al. studies) with IUCN threat status.

claims.claim: Nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181) are jeopardized by habitat degradation.
claims.source_text: In coastal, estuarine, and riverine habitats, four principal processes of habitat degradation (residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, river engineering, and pollution) jeopardize nearly one-third of threatened sharks and rays (29.8%, n = 54 of 181
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting habitat degradation threats.

claims.claim: Over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
claims.source_text: The combined effects of overexploitation and habitat degradation are most acute in freshwater, where over one-third (36.0%) of the 90 obligate and euryhaline freshwater chondrichthyans are threatened.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct count from freshwater species threat assessments.

claims.claim: Habitat degradation threatens 14% of sharks and rays through residential and commercial development, mangrove destruction, dam construction, and pollution.
claims.source_text: Specifically, the degradation of coastal, estuarine and riverine habitats threatened 14% of sharks and rays: through residential and commercial development (22 species, including river sharks Glyphis spp.); mangrove destruction for shrimp farming in Southeast Asia (4 species, including Bleeker's variegated stingray Himantura undulata); dam construction and water control (8 species, including Mekong freshwater stingray Dasyatis laosensis), and pollution (20 species).
claims.evidence_reasoning: Count of species affected by specific habitat degradation threats from IUCN assessments.

claims.claim: Population control and persecution has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 chondrichthyan species.
claims.source_text: Population control of sharks, in particular due to their perceived risk to people, fishing gear, and other fisheries has contributed to the threatened status of at least 12 species
claims.evidence_reasoning: Count from threat coding in IUCN assessments documenting persecution as a threat.

claims.claim: The threatened status of only one chondrichthyan species (New Caledonia catshark) has been directly linked to climate change.
claims.source_text: So far the threatened status of only one species has been directly linked to climate change (New Caledonia catshark Aulohalaelurus kanakorum
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on threat coding in IUCN assessment for this specific species.

claims.claim: Maximum body size is the most important predictor of chondrichthyan extinction risk.
claims.source_text: Maximum body size is an essential predictor of threat status, we presume because of the close relationship between body size and the intrinsic rate of population increase in sharks and rays
claims.evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling (Table 3, Figure 3) shows body size as strongest predictor, with mechanistic explanation supported by citations to Smith et al., 1998; Frisk et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) is an important risk factor for chondrichthyan extinction.
claims.source_text: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors
claims.evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling showing minimum depth as significant predictor in GLMMs (Tables 3, 9).

claims.claim: Narrowness of depth range is an important risk factor for chondrichthyan extinction.
claims.source_text: The shallowness of species (minimum depth limit) and the narrowness of their depth range are important risk factors
claims.evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling showing depth range as significant predictor in GLMMs (Tables 3, 9).

claims.claim: Shallow species are more accessible to fishing gears, increasing their extinction risk.
claims.source_text: We hypothesize that this is so because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Mechanistic hypothesis explaining statistical pattern, based on understanding of fishing gear accessibility.

claims.claim: Species with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that part of their population remains beyond fishing activity.
claims.source_text: We hypothesize that this is so because shallower species are more accessible to fishing gears and those with narrower depth ranges have lower likelihood that a proportion of the species distribution remains beyond fishing activity.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Mechanistic hypothesis explaining statistical pattern of depth range as risk factor.

claims.claim: Geographic range size (Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to chondrichthyan extinction risk.
claims.source_text: We find that geographic range (measured as Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to extinction risk.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Statistical modeling (Table 9E) shows geographic range has non-significant effect on threat probability.

claims.claim: The lack of relationship between geographic range and extinction risk in chondrichthyans contrasts with patterns on land and in the marine fossil record.
claims.source_text: This is in marked contrast to extinction risk patterns on land (Jones et al., 2003; Cardillo et al., 2005; Anderson et al., 2011a) and in the marine fossil record (Harnik et al., 2012a, 2012b), where small geographic range size is the principal correlate of extinction risk.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison of current findings with published patterns from terrestrial and paleontological studies.

claims.claim: Fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans, exposing even wide-ranging species.
claims.source_text: We suggest that this is because fishing activity is now widespread throughout the world's oceans (Swartz et al., 2010), and even species with the largest ranges are exposed and often entirely encompassed by the footprint of fishing activity.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Explanation for lack of range-risk relationship, supported by citation to Swartz et al., 2010 on fishing footprint.

claims.claim: Fishing has a narrow depth penetration, allowing deeper species to find refuge from exploitation.
claims.source_text: By contrast, with a few exceptions (mainly eastern Atlantic slopes, Figure 7E), fishing has a narrow depth penetration and hence species found at greater depths can still find refuge from exploitation
claims.evidence_reasoning: Explanation for depth as key risk factor, supported by citations to Morato et al., 2006; Lam and Sadovy de Mitcheson, 2010.

claims.claim: The status of chondrichthyans is among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage, apart from amphibians.
claims.source_text: The status of chondrichthyans is arguably among the worst reported for any major vertebrate lineage considered thus far, apart from amphibians
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison with other vertebrate groups from Hoffmann et al., 2010 and Stuart et al., 2004.

claims.claim: More than 30% of amphibians are threatened.
claims.source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments (Stuart et al., 2004; Hoffmann et al., 2010).

claims.claim: 38% of amphibians are Least Concern.
claims.source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments.

claims.claim: 32% of amphibians are Data Deficient.
claims.source_text: The percentage and absolute number of threatened amphibians is high (>30% are threatened), but a greater percentage are Least Concern (38%), and uncertainty of status is lower (32% DD) than for chondrichthyans.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Data from cited amphibian assessments.

claims.claim: The high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with intense extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species.
claims.source_text: Our discovery of the high level of threat in freshwater chondrichthyans (36%) is consistent with the emerging picture of the intense and unmanaged extinction risk faced by many freshwater and estuarine species
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison with broader freshwater biodiversity patterns from Darwall et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The chondrichthyan threat estimate (>24%) is distinctly greater than estimates from global fisheries risk assessments for teleost fishes.
claims.source_text: The predicted level of chondrichthyan threat (>24%) is distinctly greater than that provided by global fisheries risk assessments. These studies provide modeled estimates of the percentage of collapsed bony fish (teleost) stocks in both data-poor unassessed fisheries (18%, Costello et al., 2012) and data-rich fisheries (7–13%, Branch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison of current findings with published fisheries assessments.

claims.claim: Teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs.
claims.source_text: This could be because teleosts are generally more resilient than elasmobranchs (Hutchings et al., 2012)
claims.evidence_reasoning: Explanation for difference in threat levels, supported by citation to comparative life history study.

claims.claim: Analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries.
claims.source_text: we caution that analyses of biased geographic and taxonomic samples may be underestimating risk of collapse in global fisheries, particularly for species with less-resilient life histories.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Cautionary interpretation about potential biases in fisheries assessments based on comparison with current findings.

claims.claim: The median biomass of 112 shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
claims.source_text: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries. Assuming BMSY occurs at 0.3 to 0.5 of unexploited biomass then the median biomass of shark and ray fisheries had declined by between 81% and 89% by 2009.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Calculation based on data from Costello et al., 2012 with assumptions about BMSY.

claims.claim: Sharks and rays are the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
claims.source_text: The median biomass relative to the biomass at Maximum Sustainable Yield (B/BMSY) of these 112 shark and ray fisheries was 0.37, making them the most overfished groups of any of the world's unassessed fisheries.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct statement from Costello et al., 2012 analysis.

claims.claim: At least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct.
claims.source_text: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct
claims.evidence_reasoning: Count from assessments and literature review (Dulvy et al., 2003; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).

claims.claim: No chondrichthyan species has been driven to global extinction.
claims.source_text: While no species has been driven to global extinction—as far as we know—at least 28 populations of sawfishes, skates, and angel sharks are locally or regionally extinct
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on comprehensive assessment of all species, though qualified with 'as far as we know'.

claims.claim: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark has not been seen since 1979.
claims.source_text: The Critically Endangered Pondicherry shark (Carcharhinus hemiodon) is known only from 20 museum specimens that were captured in the heavily-fished inshore waters of Southeast Asia: it has not been seen since 1979
claims.evidence_reasoning: Information from species assessment and museum records (Cavanagh et al., 2003).

claims.claim: The Common skate is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
claims.source_text: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on regional assessments and literature (Cavanagh and Gibson, 2007; Gibson et al., 2008; Iglésias et al., 2010).

claims.claim: The Common angel shark is regionally extinct from much of its former geographic range in European waters.
claims.source_text: The now ironically-named and Critically Endangered Common skate (Dipturus batis) and Common angel shark (Squatina squatina) are regionally extinct from much of their former geographic range in European waters

claims.claim: The Largetooth sawfish is possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa.
claims.source_text: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on assessments and regional studies (Robillard and Séret, 2006; Harrison and Dulvy, 2014).

claims.claim: The Smalltooth sawfish is possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa.
claims.source_text: The Largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and Smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) are possibly extinct throughout much of the Eastern Atlantic, particularly in West Africa
claims.evidence_reasoning: Based on assessments and regional studies.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans arose at least 420 million years ago.
claims.source_text: Chondrichthyans make up one of the oldest and most ecologically diverse vertebrate lineages: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs
claims.evidence_reasoning: Established paleontological knowledge cited from Compagno, 1990; Kriwet et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans rapidly radiated to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs.
claims.source_text: they arose at least 420 million years ago and rapidly radiated out to occupy the upper tiers of aquatic food webs
claims.evidence_reasoning: Established evolutionary and ecological knowledge from cited sources.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function.
claims.source_text: Today, this group is one of the most speciose lineages of predators on earth that play important functional roles in the top-down control of coastal and oceanic ecosystem structure and function
claims.evidence_reasoning: Ecological role supported by citations to Ferretti et al., 2010; Heithaus et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates.
claims.source_text: Sharks and their relatives include some of the latest maturing and slowest reproducing of all vertebrates, exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom
claims.evidence_reasoning: Life history characteristics documented in Cortés, 2000.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit the longest gestation periods in the animal kingdom.
claims.source_text: exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom.
claims.source_text: exhibiting the longest gestation periods and some of the highest levels of maternal investment in the animal kingdom
claims.evidence_reasoning: Life history characteristics documented in Cortés, 2000.

claims.claim: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates.
claims.source_text: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival, rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality
claims.evidence_reasoning: Population dynamics principles supported by multiple citations (Musick, 1999b; Cortés, 2002; García et al., 2008; Dulvy and Forrest, 2010).

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans exhibit weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival.
claims.source_text: The extreme life histories of many chondrichthyans result in very low population growth rates and weak density-dependent compensation in juvenile survival
claims.evidence_reasoning: Population dynamics principle from cited literature.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans are intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality.
claims.source_text: rendering them intrinsically sensitive to elevated fishing mortality
claims.evidence_reasoning: Conclusion from life history characteristics, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle, particularly the Gulf of Thailand, is a hotspot of greatest residual threat for chondrichthyans.
claims.source_text: The Indo-Pacific Biodiversity Triangle, particularly the Gulf of Thailand, and the islands of Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and Sulawesi, is a hotspot of greatest residual threat especially for coastal sharks and rays with 76 threatened species
claims.evidence_reasoning: Spatial analysis showing residual threat after controlling for species richness (Figure 9).

claims.claim: The Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km².
claims.source_text: Indeed, the Gulf of Thailand large marine ecosystem has the highest threat density with 48 threatened chondrichthyans in an area of 0.36 million km2.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Calculation from spatial analysis of threatened species distributions.

claims.claim: The Red Sea is a residual threat hotspot with 29 threatened pelagic and coastal species.
claims.source_text: The Red Sea residual threat hotspot has 29 threatened pelagic and coastal species
claims.evidence_reasoning: Count from spatial analysis (Figure 9).

claims.claim: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic chondrichthyan species.
claims.source_text: There are 15 irreplaceable marine hotspots that harbor all 66 threatened endemic species
claims.evidence_reasoning: Spatial analysis of endemism and irreplaceability (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Throughout much of the pelagic ocean, 86% of chondrichthyan species are threatened or Near Threatened.
claims.source_text: Throughout much of the pelagic ocean, threat is greater than expected based on species richness alone, species richness is low (n = 30) and a high percentage (86%) are threatened (n = 16) or Near Threatened (n = 10).
claims.evidence_reasoning: Count from pelagic species assessments.

claims.claim: Only four pelagic chondrichthyan species are of Least Concern.
claims.source_text: Only four are of Least Concern (Salmon shark Lamna ditropis, Goblin shark Mitsukurina owstoni, Longnose pygmy Shark Heteroscymnoides marleyi, and Largetooth cookiecutter shark Isistius plutodus)
claims.evidence_reasoning: Direct count from pelagic species assessments.

claims.claim: Over half of chondrichthyan species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (53.9%).
claims.source_text: Over half of species are predicted to be threatened or Near Threatened (n = 561, 53.9%, Table 1).
claims.evidence_reasoning: Sum of predicted threatened (249) and Near Threatened (312) species.

claims.claim: Chondrichthyans have one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon assessed to date.
claims.source_text: A very high percentage of species are DD (46%, 487 species); that is one of the highest rates of Data Deficiency of any taxon to date
claims.evidence_reasoning: Comparison with other taxa from Hoffmann et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Coastal species are more exposed to the combined threats of fishing and habitat degradation than offshore species.
claims.source_text: Coastal species are more exposed to the combined threats of fishing and habitat degradation than those offshore in pelagic and deepwater ecosystems.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Pattern from habitat-specific threat analysis (Table 2) and spatial analysis.

claims.claim: Coastal and continental shelf chondrichthyans greater than 1 m total length have more than 50% chance of being threatened.
claims.source_text: Coastal and continental shelf and pelagic species greater than 1 m total length have a more than 50% chance of being threatened, compared to ∼12% risk for a similar-sized deepwater species

claims.claim: Pelagic chondrichthyans greater than 1 m total length have more than 50% chance of being threatened.

claims.claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans of similar size (>1 m) have approximately 12% risk of being threatened.

claims.evidence_reasoning: Prediction from GLMM models (Figure 5, Table 9).

claims.claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than shallow-water relatives due to slow growth and lower productivity.
claims.source_text: While deepwater chondrichthyans, due to their slow growth and lower productivity, are intrinsically more sensitive to overfishing than their shallow-water relatives (García et al., 2008; Simpfendorfer and Kyne, 2009) for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries
claims.evidence_reasoning: Life history principle from cited literature.

claims.claim: Deepwater chondrichthyans are less threatened than shallow-water species of similar size because they are inaccessible to most fisheries.
claims.source_text: for a given body size they are less threatened—largely because they are inaccessible to most fisheries
claims.evidence_reasoning: Explanation for pattern observed in statistical models (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) were assessed using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.
claims.source_text: We assessed most threatened chondrichthyans (81%, n = 148 of 181) using the Red List population reduction over time Criterion A.

claims.claim: 4 threatened chondrichthyan species were assessed using the small population size and decline Criterion C.

claims.evidence_reasoning: Count and species list from IUCN assessment criteria used.

claims.claim: One-third of all chondrichthyan species have been described in the past thirty years.
claims.source_text: One-third of all species have been described in the past thirty years.

claims.claim: 21 new chondrichthyan species were described in 2006.

claims.evidence_reasoning: Count of workshop participants and countries represented (Table 8).

claims.claim: Bans on 'finning' are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
claims.source_text: Bans on 'finning' (slicing off a shark's fins and discarding the body at sea) are the most widespread shark conservation measures.
claims.evidence_reasoning: Assessment of global conservation measures from review of RFMO actions.

claims.claim: Finning bans have not significantly reduced shark mortality or risk to threatened species.

claims.claim: Many governments lack the resources, expertise, and political will to effectively conserve sharks and rays.

results.result: The authors estimate that one-quarter (24%) of chondrichthyan species are threatened globally, based on IUCN Red List assessments of 1,041 species combined with predictive modeling for Data Deficient species. Of assessed species, 17.4% (181 species) are directly classified as threatened (25 CR, 43 EN, 113 VU), with an additional 68 DD species predicted to be threatened through statistical modeling.
results.result_reasoning: The threat assessment is based on systematic expert evaluation through 17 workshops with 300+ experts (C92, C93) using standardized IUCN criteria. The predictive modeling approach (C17) is methodologically sound, using body size and geographic distribution to estimate threat status of DD species. The 46.8% DD rate (C16) is acknowledged as high uncertainty, but the authors appropriately use conservative prediction methods and validate their approach against independent fisheries data (C109, C110).

results.result: Overfishing (both targeted and incidental) is identified as the primary threat to chondrichthyans, with one-third of threatened species subject to targeted fishing and others declining due to bycatch. Half (53.6%) of the 69 high-value species in the global fin trade are threatened.
results.result_reasoning: The threat attribution is based on systematic threat coding in IUCN assessments by expert panels (C2). The specific proportions for targeted vs. incidental capture (C24, C25) come directly from threat assessment data. The fin trade analysis (C26) cross-references independently documented trade species with threat status, providing convergent evidence for overfishing as the primary driver.

results.result: Large-bodied, shallow-water chondrichthyan species face the greatest extinction risk, with maximum body size and minimum depth being the strongest predictors of threat status. Coastal/shelf and pelagic species >1 m have >50% probability of being threatened, compared to ~12% for similar-sized deepwater species. Five of seven most threatened families are rays, with sawfishes (Pristidae) being the most threatened family.
results.result_reasoning: The result is supported by rigorous statistical modeling using GLMMs with phylogenetic controls (Tables 3, 9, Figure 3). The body size and depth effects are statistically significant with clear mechanistic explanations (C35, C36). The family-level patterns (C4, C22) are derived from direct counts in threat assessments. The >50% threat probability for large shallow species (C76, C77) comes from validated predictive models with high accuracy (AUC values in Table 3).

results.result: Geographic range size (Extent of Occurrence) is largely unrelated to chondrichthyan extinction risk, contrasting with terrestrial patterns where small range size predicts extinction. This is attributed to the widespread distribution of fishing activity throughout the world's oceans, while fishing has narrow depth penetration allowing deeper species refuge.
